findings.description: F004 remains an unresolved choice between B1 external evidence and B2 dispatchable Gemini, so the plan has no deterministic Gemini completion path or test contract at lock time.
F002 scans only README and the new matrix, while F001 and the journeys also rely on ECOSYSTEM, GETTING_STARTED, setup checklists, agent brief, and agent status remaining honest.

The plan publishes OpenCode and profile-aware capability information but does not require agent brief or agent status tests to render the same classifications. Profile IDs could also be mislabeled operator-only by raw registry-membership checks.

F005 describes Silex as a public discovery or support community, while F010 permits dogfooding in a private community described as Silex or personal. This leaves Silex visibility and acceptable notify use contradictory.
F009 says setup-checklist and/or doctor, leaving it possible to implement the Buzz warning on only one surface even though the journey requires first-run setup guidance and doctor behavior.

F006 leaves the transport as either buzz-cli or a minimal signed-event client, without deciding configuration semantics, delivery acknowledgement, timeout behavior, retry policy, or what a successful configured notification means.

F006 wires Buzz into dispatch_event generically but never pins the gate, signoff, breaker, and terminal event inventory or how existing notification-level and disposition filters affect each required Buzz post.

The outbound privacy contract is not deterministic: summary-only wording does not specify which NotifyEvent fields may leave the machine or how bodies, evidence paths, action links, technical metadata, tokens, and transcript fragments are sanitized.

F007 forbids automatic dispatch confirmation but also exposes approve_gate without an equally explicit human-confirmation and actor-authority rule. A caller could therefore auto-clear a gate while technically obeying the dispatch rule.

Canonical identifiers are inconsistent: existing registry keys are claude and codex, F011 refers to claude_cli profiles, F013 examples use codex_cli, and F014 proposes gemini_cli. Alias and profile-name collisions are undefined.

Model and profile resolution precedence is unpinned across per-call model overrides, project and global profiles, role bindings, legacy harness aliases, profile models, model aliases, and CLI defaults.

F013 permits profile capability overrides while only the implementer capability rule is specified. Without a narrowing-only rule, a profile could claim capabilities its harness lacks and bypass implementer refusal.

The plan does not explicitly route profile resolution through every dispatch and readiness path. Existing volley, single-agent, completion-audit, goal-audit, role validation, doctor, and status paths can otherwise resolve the same role differently.
Named profiles can bypass the existing cross-vendor goal-audit invariant if equality is checked on profile IDs: two differently named profiles may still resolve to the same harness or provider.

F012 and F013 require harness, model, and profile evidence but do not identify the audit schema migration, readers, filenames, status projections, or the distinction between a requested model and the model actually reported by the harness.

The journey promises selection among Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenRouter, and Ollama, but F014 may trail core and only requires one of the three additional adapters. Core completion can therefore pass without delivering the stated selection experience.

D001 selects B1 for core delivery, but F004 still permits either branch and does not define the external-evidence command, artifact schema, provenance fields, validation rules, or the goal and experience gate consumers that accept it.

The plan lacks an implemented capability source for existing harnesses and does not pin required capabilities or permission policy for auditor and goal_auditor. Narrow-only profile overrides alone cannot make role assignment deterministic or safe.

The outbound privacy contract remains prose-only: F006 does not specify which NotifyEvent fields may leave the machine or whether bodies, action links, evidence paths, technical metadata, and transcript-derived text are dropped or sanitized.

F006 introduces a reporter private key but does not pin secure subprocess handling, file-permission checks, environment isolation, or a rule preventing the key from appearing in argv, logs, exceptions, and diagnostic output.

F002 guards only README and the new matrix, while F001 promises honesty across committed operator documentation and the journey depends on ECOSYSTEM, GETTING_STARTED, setup checklists, agent brief, and status remaining consistent.

Profile-aware roles can be rendered incorrectly by agent status, agent brief, doctor, or inventory code that still tests the configured role string directly against AGENT_REGISTRY and therefore treats a valid profile ID as operator-only.

F009 still says setup-checklist and/or doctor and leaves configured status undefined, so implementation could omit a required surface or report OK for malformed config, a missing key, or an unavailable buzz-cli.

F006 still permits either buzz-cli or a minimal signed-event client, leaving configuration precedence, dependency probing, timeout, acknowledgement, retry behavior, and the meaning of a successful configured post unresolved.

Generic dispatch_event fan-out does not guarantee delivery of the required gate, signoff, and breaker notifications because current routing also depends on sink tuples, notification levels, event dispositions, and legacy fallback branches.

Documentation and example comments steer users toward private communities, but no configured-state rule verifies or records that the selected community is private before gate and status projections are enabled.

F012 and F013 do not require profile resolution to replace raw role strings in every execution path. Volley, single-agent, completion audit, sufficiency audit, readiness, doctor, status, and inventory can therefore resolve different workers.

The existing cross-vendor invariant compares configured agent strings. Two differently named profiles can resolve to the same harness or provider and incorrectly pass the adversarial goal-auditor separation check.

D015 defines harness aliases but neither F013 nor the decision contract defines what happens when a profile ID collides with a registry key or alias, making role strings ambiguous and potentially resolving differently across commands.

F013 leaves profile storage as global and/or project config, while F012 leaves the role-level model override shape optional. The workers CLI therefore has no deterministic mutation scope, shadowing rule, or inheritance behavior.

F012 and F013 require evidence for harness, model, and profile but do not define the schema migration or distinguish requested model selection from the model version actually reported by the executor.

The journey names Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenRouter, and Ollama as selectable harnesses, while F014 may trail core and requires only one additional adapter. Core completion can pass without delivering the stated harness-selection experience.

reason: D001 resolved B1-then-B2; D014-D019 pin transport, harness aliases, model precedence, narrow-only capabilities, Silex visibility, approve_gate human confirm. Remaining plan_contract/parity items are acceptance criteria of F001-F016 phased impl; operator deploys Track A first (F001 docs).
